problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3{x}^{2}+2)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8+4-0 \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{49}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{25}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =25 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $5\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-5=2\,m/s.
$$
